title: Nepal’s Judicial Council appoints judges to high courts while leaving Supreme Court vacancies unfilled - ua.news
description: Nepal’s Judicial Council appoints judges to high courts while leaving Supreme Court vacancies unfilled  ua.news
publisher.title: ua.news
full_article:
In Nepal, the Judicial Council has begun filling vacancies in the high courts while leaving four positions unfilled at the Supreme Court, where about 29,000 cases are pending. This was reported by The Kathmandu Post.

At a meeting chaired by Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma, the council appointed Bhadrakali Pokharel, Himlal Belbase and Gajendra Bahadur Singh as high court judges in Surkhet, Janakpur and Biratnagar, respectively. Belbase is due to retire on age grounds in four days, while Pokharel was appointed a judge on the eve of his retirement from the post of Supreme Court registrar.

Supreme Court administrative official Bharat Kumar Dahal was also appointed a district court judge and assigned to the Kailali District Court. The council transferred several other judges to high and district courts.

Supreme Court workload

On Tuesday, 489 cases were listed for hearing at the Supreme Court. Decisions were made in 230 of them, while 259 were postponed for various reasons, including the impossibility or impracticality of hearing them. Constitutionally, the court must consist of 21 judges including the chief justice, but only 17 are currently serving. Justice Binod Sharma is due to retire on age grounds next month, which will further reduce the court’s composition.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Kedar Koirala, general secretary of the Nepal Bar Association, criticized the sequence of appointments. According to him, the council resolved an administrative matter rather than the judiciary’s most urgent problem, since the shortage of Supreme Court judges directly affects parties to court proceedings.

Further personnel decisions

Manoj Kumar Sharma said that the appointment process had already begun and vacancies at all levels of the judiciary would soon be filled. At the same time, a member of the Judicial Council told the publication that appointments of Supreme Court judges and chief judges of high courts were unlikely to take place before October 1.

Full appointments to the Supreme Court have not been made for several years. In June 2025, the Judicial Council recommended Meghraj Pokharel for the post of Supreme Court justice, but one vacancy remained unfilled at that time. Subsequently, Justices Kumar Chudal and Prakash Man Singh Raut retired in October 2025 and April 2026, respectively. The Judicial Council Act of 2016 provides for recommending candidates at least one month before a judge’s planned age-based retirement.

After the meeting, the Judicial Service Commission also recommended Baburam Dahal and Thagindra Kattel for the posts of Supreme Court registrars, and Rama Prasad Bhattarai for the post of Judicial Council secretary. These appointments will take effect after government approval.

title: Mary Slusser’s secret loot of Nepal’s sacred art and heritage - Himal Southasian
description: Mary Slusser’s secret loot of Nepal’s sacred art and heritage  Himal Southasian
publisher.title: Himal Southasian
full_article:
MARY SHEPHERD SLUSSER landed in Kathmandu on 13 November 1965. She was carrying a typewriter, a pair of cats named Latsa and Bratsa, and two Persian rugs she had purchased in Tehran during a layover on her flight from Washington DC. Her husband, Harry Robert (“Bob”) Slusser, had been appointed the local deputy director of the Investment Generation Division at the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). He would help Nepal manage its timber, electrify its cities and solicit foreign investment for tourism projects.

Slusser was astounded at the beauty of her new home. She “almost screamed, yelled, and fell out of the car” as the couple drove through the centre of Kathmandu on the way to their new apartment, passing “temples and stupas and shrines and houses jumbled together and sprinkled with hill peoples, holy men, sacred cattle, scrawny dogs, scavenger pigs and heaven knows what.” In her first letter home, Slusser described Nepal as being “beyond our wildest dreams.”

Slusser bought her first stolen gods just a few weeks after she arrived. Taking a Sunday sight-seeing drive, the Slussers stopped at the Gokarneshwor Mahadev temple, dedicated to the Hindu deity Shiva, on the northeastern edge of the Kathmandu Valley. On the wide steps leading down from the temple to the Bagmati River, Slusser recorded in her diary, families were picnicking, little girls were washing brass pots and “some sort of esoteric ceremony” was in progress, “with much mutual blessings.”

This is a Himal Investigation. To see more of our investigative work, click here. To watch a behind-the-scenes conversation on the making of this story between Erin L Thompson and Himal ’s Editor, Roman Gautam, click here.

As the Slussers lingered in the temple complex’s courtyard, some boys showed them a tiny bronze sculpture of Shiva and his consort, Parvati. Slusser was “sure they had just stolen” this idol, since grains of rice, offered to the gods by their worshippers, were still clinging to its surface.

Thanks to Slusser’s intensive Nepali lessons, she understood that the boys were asking for NPR 22 for the sculpture. She bargained them down to NPR 14 – then the equivalent of USD 1.82, as she noted with customary exactitude in her diary. “It is really a very sweet piece,” she added, “and I don’t think the temple will miss it at all.”

title: Prayer for Nepal Urges Asia to Turn Solidarity into Disaster Recovery and Climate Action - Radio Veritas Asia
description: Prayer for Nepal Urges Asia to Turn Solidarity into Disaster Recovery and Climate Action  Radio Veritas Asia
publisher.title: Radio Veritas Asia
full_article:
More than 150 people from across Asia joined an interfaith prayer gathering for Nepal on September 15, turning prayers for communities affected by devastating floods and landslides into a call for concrete solidarity, compassionate service and care for creation.

The online gathering was organized by the Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences–Office of Human Development (FABC-OHD), Radio Veritas Asia and the Laudato Si’ Movement Asia Pacific, together with its chapters in Myanmar, Indonesia, Korea, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

Participants were invited to “mourn, listen, stand with and hope” with the people of Nepal, while reflecting on how prayer could lead to practical support for affected communities.

Speaking from Nepal, Jesuit priest Fr. Dr. Boby Joseph Thadathil, SJ, Superior of St. Xavier’s School in Kathmandu, described the disaster as a moment to put compassion into service.

“This is a time to show humanity, compassion, and service,” he said.

Fr. Boby said the disaster had affected not only lives and property but also homes, livelihoods, education, health care, water systems and other essential services. He called for continued solidarity during the long process of recovery and rebuilding.

He highlighted the needs of children who had lost parents and families struggling to secure shelter, food, health care and safe drinking water. He urged communities outside Nepal to provide practical support in areas including housing, education, psychosocial care, livelihoods, sanitation and disaster preparedness.

Sr. Cecilia Shrestha, SJC, Director of Caritas Nepal, linked the disaster to the growing vulnerability of communities to climate-related hazards.

“Climate change is no longer a distant or future threat for Nepalese communities, it is already affecting lives, livelihoods, food security, and displacement,” she said.

title: How an ice-rock avalanche caused the deadly China-Nepal floods - AFP Fact Check
description: How an ice-rock avalanche caused the deadly China-Nepal floods  AFP Fact Check
publisher.title: AFP Fact Check
full_article:
"Chinese illogical dam constructions in the Himalayan region (have) caused this biblical disaster!" reads an X post published on August 29, 2026.

The post shares purported satellite imagery of mountainous terrain in Nepal.

Similar claims blaming Beijing for the disaster surfaced on social media as scientists worked to determine the sequence of events that culminated in the August 26 floods, which buried entire communities and left hundreds of hydropower workers missing (archived link).



Other online narratives falsely blamed the tragedy on weather manipulation and shared fabricated videos supposedly showing what caused the deadly flooding.

Image Screenshots of false posts captured on September 11, 2026, with red crosses added by AFP

Much of the speculation stems from a vast Chinese hydropower dam being built in southeastern Tibet.

Critics of the controversial Medog Hydropower Station project have warned that building a colossal dam in one of the world's most seismically active regions could pose ecological risks to a waterway that supplies nearly two billion people downstream (archived here, here and here).

Its construction, estimated to cost $168 billion, officially began in July 2025; Beijing has provided few details, however, about what would be the world's largest hydropower dam (archived here and here).

The project seeks to construct five cascade hydropower stations on the lower reaches of the transboundary Yarlung Tsangpo river (archived link).

Hydropower construction on the river has long been a source of geopolitical tension, raising concerns in neighbouring India about potential impacts on flood control and water availability (archived here and here).

But the recent China-Nepal floods were not caused by a dam failure, as conspiracy theories online allege.

Deadly flash flooding likely occurred after part of a glacier and bedrock in Nepal's Langtang National Park broke off near the Chinese border, according to the US Geological Survey (archived link).

Image Infographic with 3D representation of satellite images showing Langtang Lirung mountain peak in Nepal, where a glacial and mountain collapse caused deadly floods in Tibet and Nepal on August 26, according to scientists (AFP / Sophie RAMIS, Luca MATTEUCCI)

Daniel Shugar, a University of Calgary geomorphologist investigating the floods, said in a September 7 email that researchers can "confidently trace the source of the disaster to a landslide composed mostly of bedrock, with some glacial ice" -- a phenomenon known as an ice-rock avalanche (archived here and here).

The large, dense mass fell thousands of metres. The combined force of the pulverised ice created a fast-moving debris flow that descended into rivers and tore through local villages.

"We don't need to resort to conspiracy theories to explain this horrific disaster," said Shugar, one of the first experts to suggest a glacial collapse as a plausible trigger.

How the floods began

AFP reviewed user-generated content (UGC), analysed satellite imagery and spoke to five experts on an international team examining the disaster's cause to break down the sequence of events that led to the devastation (archived link).

April 25, 2015: Avalanches and landslides strike Nepal's Langtang Lirung peak after the 7.8-magnitude Gorkha earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people (archived here, here and here).

Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz in Austria, told AFP on September 7 that widening cracks "eventually grew too large for the rock to hold together" (archived link).

Image Map and factfile on the 7.8-magnitude quake that hit Nepal on April 25, 2015 (AFP / Gal ROMA, AFP)

Days before August 26, 2026: Geophysicist Manoochehr Shirzaei notices the slope of Langtang Lirung peak creeping downhill, with movement accelerating in the days immediately before the collapse (archived link). The science journal Nature later covers the Virginia Tech professor's findings (archived link).

Image This handout satellite image taken by Planet Labs on August 12, 2026 and released on August 28, 2026 shows the glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal before its collapse (2026 Planet Labs PBC / Handout)

August 24: Satellite imagery shows meltwater in the area turning visibly brown and a crack propagating into the surrounding bedrock, according to a rapid assessment from HiRISK, a consortium of experts from high mountain Asia (archived here and here).

August 26, 8:37 am local time (0252 GMT): A large chunk of bedrock on Langtang Lirung peak collapses along with glacial ice.

The USGS initially registers a magnitude-4.4 earthquake but later revises its findings, attributing the signal to a slope failure involving a glacier that generated energy equivalent to a magnitude-5.2 landslide (archived link).

Seismic records show the initial collapse transitioned directly into a fast-moving flow (archived link). Satellite imagery depicts a fresh scar on the north side of Langtang Lirung peak, from which rock and ice broke off.

Image This handout satellite image released by Planet Labs on August 28, 2026 shows the chunk of glacier that collapsed near Langtang Lirung peak, with the newly formed scar highlighted in yellow by AFP (2026 Planet Labs PBC / Handout)

August 26, 8:44 am (0259 GMT): Over the next seven minutes, the ice-rock avalanche descends thousands of metres into the Lhende Khola river (archived link).

The massive flow reaches Gyirong Port, a border crossing in western China's Tibet Autonomous Region, engulfing buildings.

AFP-verified footage of the devastation circulates on Chinese social media before being removed.

August 26, 9:15-9:25 am (0330-0340 GMT): Floodwaters strike the trading settlement of Timure before barreling through several towns downstream -- including Syabrubesi and Betrawati, according to a joint rapid situation analysis report (archived link).

The debris flow destroys mountain valleys and several hydropower plants along its deadly path.

Image Screenshot of UGC footage from Newsflare showing a greenhouse surrounded by floodwaters in the town of Nuwakot in Nepal's Bagmati province on August 26, 2026

August 26, 11-11:43 am (0515-0558 GMT): Raging waters reach central Nepal and wash away the concrete bridge over the Furke Khola river. Evacuation alerts are issued across Bagmati province.

Image Screenshot of UGC footage from Newsflare showing a bridge collapsing in Nepal's Dhading District on August 26, 2026

August 26, 4 pm (1015 GMT): The sacred town of Devghat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district records a peak water level surpassing 6.5 metres as the deluge swallows homes. The floodwaters do not subside until around 6:30 pm.

Image Screenshot of UGC footage from Newsflare depicting devastation in the town of Devghat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026

'Just not possible'

The relatively brief interval between the ice-rock avalanche and the torrent "leaves no time for a separate event", said Kristen Cook, a geomorphologist at Université Grenoble Alpes -- let alone the breaching of a large hydropower dam (archived link).

Despite the scale of China's Medog hydropower project, several experts told AFP it was physically impossible for it to have triggered the floods.

The dam is located on a different river system separated by a mountain range that flows across southeastern Tibet and eventually descends to the Ganges Delta (archived link).

Meanwhile, the Lhende Khola, where the recent floods occurred, flows from a separate river system near the northeastern border dividing Nepal and China.

"Medog is far downstream and to the east. Even in a hypothetical catastrophic failure, the water would travel away from Nepal," said Umesh Haritashya, professor of earth, environment and sustainability at the University of Dayton (archived link).

Image Infographic map showing hydropower projects along Nepal's flood-hit Trishuli river and the surrounding region (AFP / John SAEKI) Image Map showing major dam projects on the upper stream of the Brahmaputra River, Yarlung Zangbo as of April 2021 (AFP / Laurence CHU)

Had a large dam collapsed, the reservoir would have discharged a lot of sediment-poor water over a slightly longer period instead of the "short, violent, extremely sediment-rich surge" witnessed during the floods, Haritashya added.

Satellite images and maps also do not depict a Chinese dam in the flood-affected area, which experts say would be unmistakable (archived link).

"It's just not possible. You can't hide dam construction," Cook said.

Climate change's role

The floods in Nepal occurred as the region copes with climate change and increasing flood intensity (archived link).

Intensifying glacier retreat in the Himalayan region has also exposed unstable mountain slopes, increasing risks for erosion and landslides (archived link).

A combination of rapid infrastructure development and warming temperatures has exacerbated those risks, causing glaciers to retreat in recent decades, studies show.

But "the degree to which climate change caused this specific event is still unclear", Cook said.

Image Infographic showing the retreat of glaciers in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region using 1980 and 2020 data from ICIMOD (AFP / Nicholas SHEARMAN) Image Infographic showing the estimated average summer temperatures from 1970 to 2026 at the site of the August 26 glacial collapse, based on data compiled by Berkeley Earth from the European Copernicus program and a network of 14 high-altitude weather stations (AFP / Paz PIZARRO, Luca MATTEUCCI)

Simon Cook, a glaciologist and senior lecturer at the University of Dundee, also told AFP on September 7 that "it is difficult to prove that any one singular event is a consequence of climate change" (archived link).

"The attribution process is quite complex and takes time. We are certainly not there yet."

Hydropower plant risks

Beyond conspiracy theories, the China-Nepal catastrophe has reignited debate over the environmental and social impacts of large-scale development projects in the Himalayas.

Foreign companies have aggressively developed urban infrastructure in the resource-rich region, increasing by 135 percent from 1991 to 2018, according to one satellite-based study (archived link).

Hydropower plants have led to fatal disasters in the past -- notably in 1963, when a large mass collapsed into a reservoir in northern Italy (archived link). The resulting wave overtopped the Vajont Dam and killed approximately 2,000 people (archived link).

"The notion that a hydropower dam could burst or cause a flood is true, but it had absolutely nothing to do with this event," Simon Cook said of the China-Nepal disaster.

But whether such projects worsened the impact requires additional investigation, experts said.

"Hydropower construction and other forms of development have brought more people into high-risk locations," said Kristen Cook of Université Grenoble Alpes.

Deepening labour shortages and rapid depopulation in Nepal's rural districts have driven urban migration to areas such as Bagmati province, which was hardest hit by the floods (archived here and here).

More than a third of Nepal's 261 planned and operational hydropower plants are concentrated in Bagmati, according to the Nepal Hydropower Portal (archived link).

The facilities help reduce carbon emissions and are central to Nepal's economy, with hydropower responsible for 99 percent of the country's electricity generation (archived link).

But at the same time, "it is difficult to build a hydropower project in this environment that is completely safe", Kristen Cook said.

Two back-to-back earthquakes struck northwestern Nepal on Wednesday (September 16, 2026), authorities said.

However, there have been no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

According to the National Seismological Research Centre, the first tremor of magnitude 4.5 was recorded at 1:51 a.m. (local time).

The second quake, with a magnitude of 4.2, struck at 4:28 a.m. (local time), with its epicentre also located around Kalai in Mugu district, the centre said.

The shock was also felt in neighbouring districts of Dolpa and Jumla. However, there was no immediate report of any damage caused by the tremors.

Nepal, situated in a seismically active zone, frequently experiences earthquakes. The region continues to be on alert, with authorities monitoring for any aftershocks or potential structural damage in the affected areas.

title: PATA Foundation launches Nepal Tourism Recovery Fund to support tourism livelihoods - TTGmice
description: PATA Foundation launches Nepal Tourism Recovery Fund to support tourism livelihoods  TTGmice
publisher.title: TTGmice
full_article:
The PATA Foundation has launched the Nepal Tourism Recovery Fund to support tourism workers and small businesses whose livelihoods have been affected by the devastating floods that struck Nepal on August 26.

The floods caused significant loss of life and widespread damage, particularly along affected river corridors and downstream communities. Tourism communities in the affected areas, including guides, drivers, porters and operators of homestays, lodges, teahouses and small hotels, have lost homes, business premises, equipment and income.

The devastating flash floods of August 26 caused significant loss of life and widespread damage along specific river corridors in Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Trishuli areas, particularly in Rasuwa district and downstream communities

The Nepal Tourism Recovery Fund will focus on helping these tourism-dependent families and businesses rebuild their capacity to earn a living.

Donations to the Fund will support practical recovery needs, including equipment for guides, porters, drivers and tourism workers; the refitting of lodges, homestays and teahouses so they can receive guests again; tools, stock and equipment for tourism-related businesses; and shared facilities used by affected communities.

Every grant will be approved by the PATA Foundation’s Board of Trustees, with the Foundation committed to publishing information on funds raised and how they are used.

The Fund is open to contributions from individuals, tourism organisations, businesses and other supporters of Nepal’s tourism community.

To support the Nepal Tourism Recovery Fund, visit www.patafoundation.org/nepal-tourism-recovery-fund.

For organisations interested in making a direct contribution or discussing a larger commitment, please contact Foundation@PATA.org.

title: Flood death toll at Nepal-China border rises to 1,442 - Türkiye Today
description: Flood death toll at Nepal-China border rises to 1,442  Türkiye Today
publisher.title: Türkiye Today
full_article:
R escuers in Nepal recovered 14 bodies on Tuesday, raising the country's confirmed death toll to 1,399, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The authority said 5,179 people remain unaccounted for.

The agency reported that 13,742 people have been rescued since the disaster struck, with 21,022 security personnel mobilized for search, rescue and relief operations.

Among those still missing are 587 foreign tourists. Authorities noted the missing-person count remains subject to verification and may include unidentified bodies or people already rescued.

Across the border in Xizang, the Chinese autonomous region Beijing designates in place of Tibet, the death toll stands at 43, with 519 people missing, including 261 foreign nationals

Flood-damaged homes and buildings are buried in mud and debris along the Trishuli River in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, Sept. 11, 2026. (AFP Photo)

Glacier fracture triggered disaster

The disaster began Aug. 26, when a glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung, a peak in the Himalayas north of Kathmandu, fractured at an altitude of 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).

The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that turned into a massive debris flow, sweeping through valleys along the Nepal-China border.

Flood death toll at Nepal-China border rises to 1,442

Districts across Nepal affected

Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, located north and northeast of Kathmandu, as well as the Kathmandu Valley itself. On the Chinese side, the disaster buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
US Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Megan Bouldin paid a courtesy call on Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the Prime Minister’s Office in Singha Durbar on Wednesday.

During the meeting, Shah thanked the US government for expressing solidarity with Nepal and for its support at a difficult time following the disasters, according to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat.

Shah said both Nepali and foreign nationals had been affected by the disasters. He also said Nepal was confronting the impacts of climate change, stressing the need to strengthen global cooperation and collective efforts to reduce climate-related disaster risks and address their effects.

The prime minister also discussed Nepal’s tourism potential and opportunities for mutual benefit through the development of the tourism sector. He said Nepal would continue to welcome US investment.

Bouldin expressed deep sorrow over the loss of life and property caused by the floods in Rasuwa and conveyed condolences to bereaved families and affected communities.

She said the US government stood in solidarity with the government and people of Nepal at this difficult time and was ready to provide necessary assistance and cooperate in relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts.

KATHMANDU: The United States (US) has reaffirmed its support for Nepal’s recovery efforts following the devastating floods of August 26, with discussions focusing on humanitarian assistance, disaster response, and strengthening bilateral cooperation.

Chargé d’Affaires, a.i. Megan Bouldin met Prime Minister Balendra Shah today and conveyed US President Donald Trump’s offer of support to Nepal, along with the condolences and sympathies of the American people to those affected by the disaster.

During the meeting, Bouldin thanked Prime Minister Shah for his government’s assistance in the search for missing American citizens. She also highlighted the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s (FBI) ongoing cooperation with Nepal Police in identifying disaster victims, with the aim of providing answers to American and Nepali families and others awaiting information about their loved ones.

Bouldin reiterated the US commitment to working closely with the Government of Nepal on flood relief and recovery efforts. She noted that the United States has provided more than $5 million in life-saving health, humanitarian, and forensic assistance to support Nepal’s response to and recovery from the disaster.

The two sides also discussed opportunities to further expand economic and commercial cooperation, including creating greater opportunities for American and Nepali businesses. Such cooperation, they noted, can contribute to Nepal’s immediate recovery as well as its long-term economic growth.

title: Nepal Glacier Disaster Deepens India's Fears Over China's Himalayan Mega-Dam - JAPAN Forward
description: Nepal Glacier Disaster Deepens India's Fears Over China's Himalayan Mega-Dam  JAPAN Forward
publisher.title: JAPAN Forward
full_article:
A landslide near the Nepal–China border that left more than 5,500 people missing appears to have been triggered by a glacial avalanche linked to global warming, according to a new study.

As permafrost degrades across the Himalayan region and destabilizes high-altitude slopes, China's government is pressing ahead with what Premier Li Qiang has called a "project of the century"—a massive hydropower dam in the Tibet Autonomous Region—raising concern in downstream India.

The Nepal Academy of Science and Technology released a report on August 31 analyzing the disaster.

At around 8:37 AM on August 26, an estimated 100 million to 200 million cubic meters of ice and rock broke away from the northern slope of Langtang Lirung, roughly 5,200 meters above sea level on the Nepalese side of the border. The avalanche plunged into the Lhende Khola River about 2.2 kilometers below, triggering what the report described as a catastrophic debris flow.

The report characterized it as among the largest flash floods on record in Nepal caused by a glacial collapse.

Report Warns of Intensifying Flash Floods

The report cautioned that flash floods are becoming more severe and frequent in rivers fed by Himalayan glacial meltwater in Nepal. It pointed to climate warming as the underlying cause of glacier melt across the Himalayas and called for urgent protection and monitoring measures.

The Times of India newspaper drew a broader lesson from the disaster, warning that the Himalayas are becoming an increasingly hazardous region where geological and climatic constraints can no longer be ignored.

The paper raised the alarm from India's perspective over the disaster risk posed by China's construction of a hydropower station on the Yarlung Tsangpo River, which flows from the northern foothills of the Himalayas and becomes the Brahmaputra in India.

A Dam Three Times the Size of Three Gorges

China broke ground on the hydropower station in July 2025. The project carries a total investment of 1.2 trillion yuan—roughly 28 trillion yen (about $190 billion)—and is expected to generate 300 billion kilowatt-hours annually, three times the output of the Three Gorges Dam in Hubei Province, currently the world's largest.

The Times of India noted that the Yarlung Tsangpo and its tributaries, which flow through China, India and Bangladesh, sustain communities, farmland and ecosystems in northeastern India, but have also caused severe flooding at times. The paper expressed concern that China's dams, tunnels and power stations along the river could affect downstream water flow.

Fault Lines and Warnings From Chinese Researchers

The Times of India further argued that China itself is aware of the risks of building a mega dam in an earthquake-prone area. Research teams from the China Geological Survey and other institutions have found active faults at the dam site and warned that seismic activity there could easily trigger landslides and rockfalls.

Rajiv Dogra, a former Indian diplomat, put it starkly in a post on X: "A much bigger devastation could strike India's North-East if China goes to complete its 60,000 MW monster dam on Brahmaputra in a seismologically sensitive zone."

Hong Kong's South China Morning Post reported that a large-scale glacial collapse occurred at the dam site in 2021, temporarily damming the river and sharply raising water levels.

The Times of India warned that glacial collapses and earthquakes can trigger landslides that send catastrophic surges of water and debris downstream, and that roads, bridges, hydropower stations and settlements along the river could be caught up in this chain of disasters.

Water Security and Strategic Leverage

For India, which has an ongoing border dispute with China, Beijing's control over upstream flow through a mega dam is also a water-security issue. Infrastructure development near the border—including roads and communications networks—could likewise support Chinese military logistics in the event of a conflict.

A Shanghai-based security researcher told the South China Morning Post that the hydropower station could give China real diplomatic and geopolitical leverage over India.

Such considerations may well be part of Beijing's calculations.
